source.title: K-Shield: Improving the Safety-Utility Trade-off in Refusal Steering with Local Null-Space Constraints

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates a refusal-vector addition baseline on harmful-request refusal and benign-task utility, but does not specify that it uses the original difference-in-means extraction procedure or reproduce its full intervention.
record.gate_note: The RV (Ablation) baseline directly applies a refusal vector and reports behavioral outcomes, so those results bear on V1. K-Shield's own regional maps and the other steering baselines are not single-direction interventions; their results are not recorded as tests of the listed direction claims.
record.test_reason: The study reports refusal rates under its RV baseline, which adds a refusal vector to activations in three instruct models. This bears on V1's addition half: adding the direction induces refusal. The evidence is weak. The RV is a comparator in a steering-method paper. Its extraction (difference-in-means is only implied by citing Arditi and Marks & Tegmark), layers and strength are not stated. Ablation is never tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that local null-space constraints (K-Shield) improve defense and aggregate utility over global null-space steering. They present the RV baseline as an upper bound on safety with no utility constraint, illustrating a safety–utility trade-off. They make no claim about whether refusal is mediated by a single direction.
record.recipe_differences: The paper reports direct application of an RV, but does not specify its extraction procedure, layer/position scope, or whether it uses the original difference-in-means construction. It does not test direction ablation.
record.method_sensitivity: not stated for the RV baseline.
record.peer_reviewed: Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027
record.problems: For the RV results bearing on V1, no uncertainty estimates are reported. The paper does not specify how the refusal vector was obtained. Evaluation uses three instruction-tuned models and GPT-4o judging; the paper notes that broader prompt distributions and adaptive attacks require further study.
record.rows_left_out: No RV results left out. Results for K-Shield and other steering methods in Tables 1–4 and the appendices are not included as rows because they are not single-direction interventions.

untested.parts: Ablating the direction to remove refusal; capability preservation under ablation; confirmation that the vector is a difference-in-means direction; the layer and position used.
All parts. Attacks are defended against, but there is no test of whether they suppress the direction.

missing.what: The RV's extraction method, steered layers and strength are not reported anywhere. The paper says only that it 'directly applies the refusal vector'.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'challenges' label is wrong. V1's preservation of other abilities concerns ablation; adding a refusal vector to every input is expected to induce refusal and degrade task scores. The XSTest drops are induced refusal, which V1 predicts, so they support V1 rather than limit it, except for Qwen. Qwen's near-zero MATH and GSM8K under RV, with 68% XSTest compliance, suggests possible output degradation beyond refusal, but the paper does not say. Consider downgrading the relation to uses_without_test, since the RV is an underspecified comparator.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not state how the RV was derived, does not test ablating a difference-in-means direction, and does not report the all-layer/all-position ablation or addition procedure. Its benign measure is XSTest compliance, not a direct count of harmless-request refusals.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration intervention is evaluated.
The paper evaluates defenses against jailbreak attacks but does not test whether those attacks suppress the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
Local projectors and regional steering maps are evaluated, but the paper does not test whether refusal itself is affine, conic, or carried by multiple refusal directions.
No separation between harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is tested.
No transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages is tested.
The paper does not vary refusal training or test how training determines whether a removable direction exists.

relation.reason: The study reports its own refusal and compliance rates under refusal-vector addition (Tables 1-2), and these bear on whether adding the direction induces refusal.

tranche.reason: The paper does not aim at the refusal-direction question. The RV is an upper-bound baseline in a steering-defense paper. Its intervention (injecting a refusal vector, citing Arditi) is if anything the original's method, not a different one, and the recipe was judged close. The new part is the setting: jailbreak prompts and XSTest-safe, scored by a GPT-4o judge. That is a new setting with a result on V1's addition half, i.e. T3.

source_check.notes: The pack gave no [lN] ids for its verdicts, so l1-l3 here number them by their order in the pack. Appendix F gives steered layers and λ for K-Shield only; the RV's extraction, layer and strength are never stated. The judge is GPT-4o with AlphaSteer prompts; jailbreak sets have 100 prompts per attack (500 for Jailbroken), and XSTest-safe has 250. RV utility collapses (utility 30.4/19.4/2.7). On Qwen, MATH 2.0 and GSM8K 3.0 with XSTest CR 68.0 suggest damage beyond refusal. The ICLR reviewer-AI-policy footer on page 1 is venue boilerplate addressed to human reviewers, not instructions to an AI.

statements.correction: RV baseline, Table 2, XSTest safe subset (250 prompts, GPT-4o judge), compliance rate: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 92.0 -> 5.2; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 97.2 -> 68.0. RV layer, strength and derivation not stated.
statements.problem: The numbers for this study are right. Minor wording issue: 'K-Shield's refusal vector' is the paper's RV ablation baseline, not the K-Shield method. The conditions correctly say the RV derivation, layer and strength are unstated, so 'addition at one layer' is not known for this study.

statements.correction: Table 2: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, XSTest safe CR 92.0 -> 5.2 with RV; GPT-4o judge; RV extraction, layer and strength not stated.
statements.problem: none. XSTest-safe compliance 92.0% -> 5.2% on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under the RV baseline, and 'RV of unstated derivation' are both right.

reader_labels.condition: RV addition on the seven jailbreak attack sets, all three instruction-tuned models
reader_labels.reason: DSR is 100.00 for Llama and Qwen and 99.86 for Gemma after RV addition, versus the unsteered baselines (rows RV-L-DSR-avg, RV-Q-DSR-avg, RV-G-DSR-avg).

reader_labels.label: challenges

reader_labels.reason: Aggregate utility and several task scores fall markedly, contrary to the version's expectation that other abilities remain largely intact (rows RV-L-AlpacaEval through RV-G-Utility).
